deep.reconstruction:
Folio 32v contains no formulas. It is a short, heavily corrected prose draft in pencil, about eight lines, that breaks off mid-sentence. The rest of the leaf is blank.

Context from the preceding page (32r): Riemann is drafting the conceptual opening of his theory of functions of a complex variable, in the spirit of the Inaugural Dissertation (1851), §1. Take w = u + i v depending continuously on z = x + i y. For infinitesimal increments one can always write dw = a dx + b dy, a linear expression in dx and dy with coefficients a and b; this is just differentiability in the real sense. The ratio dw/dz then generally depends on the direction dy/dx. Hence the 'theorem in question' does not follow from mere continuity or the mere existence of partial differential quotients. That theorem is that dw/dz is independent of the direction of dz, i.e. the ratio of dw to the increment of x equals its ratio to the increment of iy. In modern terms (my restatement): ∂w/∂x = (1/i) ∂w/∂y, equivalently ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x, i.e. the Cauchy–Riemann equations u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x.

This page continues that methodological argument. The first line closes the previous sentence ('...[into a function of a] variable quantity is converted'). Riemann then argues roughly as follows (my paraphrase of a partly illegible text): 'If this theorem is to hold for these functions, then either it must lie in their definition, or (when one defines the function itself in some other way, e.g. through operations of computation) it would have to be proved from the concept of a function of the variable quantity; in that case this theorem would indeed ...'. The draft stops there.

The point being prepared is the one Riemann makes in the dissertation. For functions built from z by arithmetic operations, direction-independence of dw/dz is a consequence. He therefore takes it as the defining property of 'function of a complex variable quantity', instead of the formula-based (Eulerian) definition. No derivation is carried out on this page.
errors: No mathematical errors can be assessed: the page contains no computations. It is an unfinished, heavily corrected conceptual draft that ends mid-sentence.

results.what: Methodological claim that direction-independence of dw/dz (complex differentiability) must either be made part of the definition of a complex function or be proved from some other definition; Riemann opts to make it the definition.
results.modern_name: Definition of holomorphic function via complex differentiability / Cauchy–Riemann equations
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1814/1825) and d'Alembert/Euler for the equations; Riemann (Inauguraldissertation 1851) for the definition of an analytic function by this property

deep.surprise_reason: This is a preliminary draft of the well-known opening argument of Riemann's 1851 dissertation (definition of a complex function by direction-independence of the derivative). There is no new mathematical content.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); w=expand((x+I*y)**2); u=re(w); v=im(w); simplify(diff(u,x)-diff(v,y))==0 and simplify(diff(u,y)+diff(v,x))==0
checkable.asserts: For w = z^2 (a function built from z by arithmetic operations) the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold, i.e. dw/dz is independent of direction.

For w = conj(z), which is continuous with linear dw = dx - i dy, the condition dw/dy = i dw/dx fails. So continuity plus a linear differential does not imply the theorem, which is the point of the previous page.

transcription_corrections: Line 3: read 'so müsste er entweder ... in der Definition derselben liegen'. 'liegen' appears to be the intended verb of this clause (struck and/or rewritten above), with the interlinear addition 'wie sich es ... ' above it.
Line 5: 'wenn man die Function selbst definirt' — plausible, but the words after 'wenn man' are uncertain ('die Function selbst [anders?] definirt').

Line 8: 'so möchte sich dieser Satz ... allerdings' — 'dagegen' is doubtful; the reading 'so möchte [dagegen?] sich dieser Satz allerdings ...' is consistent with the image, and the sentence breaks off.
